newsitem.title: USA: NYS Assembly studies raise questions on LIPA pact.
newsitem.headline: NYS Assembly studies raise questions on LIPA pact.

text.p: The New York State Assembly, after holding hearings into a plan for a partial takeover of Long Island Lighting Co (LILCO), has taken issue with estimates of how much the deal is likely to save the utility's customers, according to two studies distributed to lawmakers.

One of the main concerns raised by the studies is whether the takeover by the state's Long Island Power Authority (LIPA) would deprive ratepayers of the benefits from any future competitive and technological developments. Long Islanders now pay some of the highest electricity rates in the United States.
Copies of the studies were provided to Reuters on Tuesday.

"The LIPA deal locks Long Islanders into a 30-year-plus period in which both competition and technology changes that could substantially lower electricity prices are unlikely to occur," one of the two studies said.
Under the deal proposed by New York Gov. George Pataki, a Republican, the authority would buy assets from a new holding company to be formed by the proposed merger of LILCO and Brooklyn Union Gas.
The consent of the Assembly, led by Democrats, is essential because it could veto the $7.26 billion bond sale needed to finance the transaction.
Pataki, a Republican, told reporters in Albany he did not know when the state bond board, which must approve all such transactions, would hold its next meeting.
The next scheduled meeting is July 16 but a special meeting could be called anytime. A spokesman for the governor was not immediately available to comment.

The Assembly said electricity customers would pay an average of $400 each in interest per year over the next 35 years. Over the life of the bonds, a ratepayer would pay about $23,000 in total debt service--$14,000 in interest and $9,000 in principal -- it said.
The Assembly included an analysis it said showed that during the first 10 years of the deal, the savings appeared to average 8.9 percent, instead of 19 percent average the state authority estimated.

The difference in estimates resulted from a number of factors, one of the papers said, noting the authority's estimates hinge on a rate stabilization plan designed to hold rates down during years three to 10 of the transaction.

A spokesman for LIPA dismissed the conclusions. "There are no new numbers in this report." Later, he added: "It's a silly thing to suggest that we're putting new debt on customers' heads. They already have to pay their electric bills." The spokesman explained the present electricity rates reflect LILCO's high costs, which the plan aims to reduce.

The Assembly also subtracted other factors in its analysis of the projected savings, such as those that LIPA expects would result from the planned merger of LILCO and Brooklyn Union. It said those savings would occur without LIPA's involvement.
LIPA's initial debt profile would reach $8.07 billion, including the cost of settling a tax case against LILCO's shuttered Shoreham nuclear plant, the Assembly said.

It added LIPA's obligations were estimated to exceed its revenues by more than $1.322 billion in the third to the 10th year. "Covering this deficit requires utilizing funds that would otherwise have reduced the need for borrowing," it added.
